banking--famous-bank-failures--t-aig-the.summary: AIG sold hundreds of billions in credit default swaps guaranteeing bank assets without holding reserves to pay claims. When the housing market collapsed, AIG's inability to pay threatened to take down every major bank it had insured.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-aig-the.whyItMatters: AIG proved that a single non-bank institution could hold the entire financial system hostage. Its $182 billion government bailout remains the largest corporate rescue in history.
takeaways: AIG sold $440 billion in credit default swaps acting as insurance on bank assets
The $182 billion bailout was necessary to prevent cascading bank failures
AIG's Financial Products division operated with virtually no regulatory oversight

faq.question: How did an insurance company threaten the entire banking system?
faq.answer: AIG sold credit default swaps that guaranteed banks' mortgage-related assets. When those assets collapsed, AIG owed billions it could not pay. If AIG defaulted, every bank holding its guarantees would have faced massive uninsured losses simultaneously.

faq.question: Was AIG's bailout money ever repaid?
faq.answer: The US government eventually recovered its full $182 billion investment plus a $22.7 billion profit by selling its AIG stock holdings, making it one of the few profitable bailouts from the financial crisis.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-barings.summary: Barings Bank, Britain's oldest merchant bank founded in 1762, was destroyed in 1995 by a single trader, Nick Leeson, who hid $1.4 billion in unauthorized losses in a secret account from his Singapore office.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-barings.whyItMatters: A 233-year-old institution was wiped out by one employee exploiting basic control failures. Barings proved that even the most prestigious banks can collapse from internal weaknesses.
takeaways: Leeson controlled both trading and back-office settlement at Barings Singapore
Losses were hidden in a secret account numbered 88888
Barings was sold to ING for one British pound after its collapse

faq.question: How did one trader destroy a 233-year-old bank?
faq.answer: Leeson held dual roles controlling both trading and settlement, allowing him to hide losses. Management trusted his reported profits and never independently verified his positions. When losses exceeded the bank's entire capital, there was nothing left.

faq.question: What banking reforms followed the Barings collapse?
faq.answer: The failure led to mandatory separation of trading and settlement functions, stronger internal audit requirements, and independent risk management oversight. It became a foundational case study in operational risk management.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-bcci-th.summary: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International was a $20 billion global bank that operated as a criminal enterprise, laundering money for drug cartels, dictators, and terrorists while bribing regulators across 73 countries.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-bcci-th.whyItMatters: BCCI exposed the dangers of a bank operating across dozens of jurisdictions with no single regulator having a complete picture. Its closure triggered reforms in international banking supervision.
takeaways: BCCI operated in 73 countries with no effective consolidated supervision
Clients included the CIA, Pablo Escobar, Saddam Hussein, and Abu Nidal
The bank was shut down simultaneously in seven countries in 1991

faq.question: How did BCCI operate as a criminal enterprise for so long?
faq.answer: BCCI deliberately structured itself across multiple jurisdictions so no single regulator could see the full picture. It was incorporated in Luxembourg, headquartered in London, and audited by two different firms for different divisions.

faq.question: What reforms resulted from the BCCI scandal?
faq.answer: The Basel Committee established requirements for consolidated supervision of international banks. Regulators gained authority to prevent banks from operating in structures designed to avoid oversight, and information sharing between supervisors improved.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-bear-st.summary: Bear Stearns was the first major Wall Street casualty of the 2008 crisis, collapsing in 72 hours when counterparties refused to trade with it. The Fed orchestrated a fire-sale purchase by JPMorgan at $10 per share, down from $170.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-bear-st.whyItMatters: Bear Stearns demonstrated how quickly confidence can vanish in modern finance. Its emergency rescue set the precedent for government intervention that would define the rest of the 2008 crisis.
takeaways: Bear Stearns collapsed in just 72 hours as counterparties pulled away
JPMorgan bought the firm at $10 per share, down from $170 six months earlier
The Fed provided $30 billion in guarantees to facilitate the deal

faq.question: Why did Bear Stearns collapse so quickly?
faq.answer: Bear Stearns relied heavily on overnight borrowing for daily operations. When rumors of trouble spread, lenders refused to roll over short-term funding and trading counterparties pulled their business, creating a fatal liquidity spiral in days.

faq.question: Why was Bear Stearns rescued but Lehman Brothers was not?
faq.answer: When Bear Stearns collapsed in March 2008, regulators feared a systemic meltdown. By September, political backlash against bailouts had grown. Lehman was allowed to fail in part because the government misjudged the consequences.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-can-we-.summary: Despite decades of regulation, stress testing, and higher capital requirements since 2008, the 2023 bank failures showed that new risks keep emerging. The question is whether the banking system can ever be made truly failure-proof.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-can-we-.whyItMatters: If bank failures are inevitable despite regulation, the focus shifts to building systems that can absorb failures without systemic damage. Understanding these limits helps set realistic expectations for financial stability.
takeaways: Post-2008 regulations significantly increased bank capital and oversight
The 2023 failures revealed risks from interest rate exposure not caught by stress tests
Complete prevention is likely impossible so containment matters more

faq.question: Why do banks keep failing despite better regulation?
faq.answer: Each crisis originates from risks that previous regulations did not anticipate. The 2008 crisis came from securitization, while 2023 failures came from interest rate risk. Regulations address past problems while future risks take new and unexpected forms.

faq.question: What approach works better than trying to prevent all failures?
faq.answer: Building a system that can absorb individual bank failures without contagion is more realistic. This means adequate deposit insurance, effective resolution mechanisms, and reducing interconnections that allow one failure to cascade across the system.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-contine.summary: Continental Illinois became the first bank officially deemed too big to fail in 1984 when the FDIC bailed out all depositors and creditors, including those above the insurance limit, to prevent a panic that could spread to other banks.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-contine.whyItMatters: Continental Illinois established the too-big-to-fail doctrine that still shapes banking today. The decision to protect all creditors created moral hazard that contributed to every subsequent banking crisis.
takeaways: Continental Illinois was the seventh-largest US bank when it failed
The FDIC protected all depositors and creditors, even those above insurance limits
The phrase too big to fail was coined during Congressional hearings on the bailout

faq.question: Why was Continental Illinois considered too big to fail?
faq.answer: Regulators found that 179 smaller banks had deposits at Continental exceeding their insurance limits. Allowing it to fail would have triggered cascading failures at these banks, potentially causing a nationwide banking panic.

faq.question: How did the Continental Illinois bailout create moral hazard?
faq.answer: By protecting all creditors, the government signaled that large bank depositors and bondholders had implicit government backing. This reduced the incentive for creditors to monitor bank risk-taking, encouraging more reckless behavior.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-cr-dit-.summary: Credit Mobilier of America was a construction company that defrauded the US government of millions during the transcontinental railroad project by overbilling for construction and bribing members of Congress to look the other way.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-cr-dit-.whyItMatters: The Credit Mobilier scandal of 1872 was one of America's first major financial corruption cases, exposing how private financial entities could capture government institutions and use public money for private enrichment.
takeaways: Credit Mobilier billed the government double the actual construction costs
Members of Congress received shares at below-market prices to ensure silence
The scandal implicated a sitting vice president and multiple congressmen

faq.question: How did the Credit Mobilier scheme work?
faq.answer: Union Pacific Railroad's insiders created Credit Mobilier as a construction company. They awarded themselves massively inflated contracts to build the railroad, pocketing the difference between actual costs and billed amounts, funded by government bonds.

faq.question: What consequences followed the Credit Mobilier scandal?
faq.answer: Two congressmen were censured, Vice President Schuyler Colfax's career was ruined, and public trust in government plummeted. The scandal contributed to calls for civil service reform and corporate accountability that shaped the Progressive Era.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-credit-.summary: Credit Suisse, once Switzerland's second-largest bank, collapsed in 2023 after years of scandals, risk management failures, and client exodus. UBS acquired it in a government-brokered emergency deal worth $3.25 billion.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-credit-.whyItMatters: Credit Suisse's failure proved that even a 167-year-old globally systemic bank could die from accumulated reputational damage. The forced merger created a Swiss megabank raising concentration concerns.
takeaways: Credit Suisse lost over $8 billion from Archegos and Greensill Capital alone
The bank experienced a $120 billion deposit outflow in the quarter before collapse
UBS acquired Credit Suisse for $3.25 billion, a fraction of book value

faq.question: What caused Credit Suisse to collapse?
faq.answer: Years of scandals including Archegos losses, Greensill exposure, Mozambique corruption, and spy scandals eroded client confidence. When depositors accelerated withdrawals in March 2023, the bank could not survive despite being well-capitalized on paper.

faq.question: Was the UBS takeover a bailout?
faq.answer: Swiss authorities insisted it was not a bailout but a commercial merger. However, the government provided $9 billion in loss guarantees to UBS and the Swiss National Bank offered $108 billion in liquidity support, making it taxpayer-backed in practice.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-deposit.summary: Deposit insurance was created in 1933 to end bank panics by guaranteeing customer deposits. While it has largely succeeded in preventing runs, critics argue it also enables reckless bank behavior by removing depositor discipline.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-deposit.whyItMatters: Deposit insurance is the foundation of modern banking confidence. Without it, bank runs would be common. But the guarantee also means depositors have no incentive to monitor whether their bank takes foolish risks.
takeaways: The FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank
Bank runs virtually disappeared after deposit insurance was introduced
The 2023 SVB crisis showed the system's limits when uninsured deposits dominate

faq.question: How does deposit insurance prevent bank runs?
faq.answer: When depositors know their money is guaranteed by the government, they have no reason to rush to withdraw during a scare. This eliminates the self-fulfilling panic where rational fear of a run causes the actual run.

faq.question: Does deposit insurance make banks take more risks?
faq.answer: Yes, this is a well-documented moral hazard. When depositors' money is guaranteed, they do not bother checking if their bank is taking excessive risks. Banks can attract deposits with high rates funded by risky investments, knowing the FDIC backs the deposits.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-first-r.summary: First Republic Bank catered to wealthy clients with below-market mortgage rates and exceptional service. When interest rates rose sharply, its portfolio of cheap mortgages lost value and wealthy depositors fled, leading to its seizure and sale to JPMorgan.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-first-r.whyItMatters: First Republic's failure showed that even a well-run bank serving wealthy clients can be destroyed by interest rate risk. Its business model of cheap mortgages for rich clients became a liability overnight.
takeaways: First Republic offered mortgages at rates well below market to attract wealthy clients
Rising rates made its low-rate mortgage portfolio worth billions less than face value
JPMorgan acquired the failed bank's assets in an FDIC-brokered deal

faq.question: Why did a bank serving wealthy clients fail?
faq.answer: First Republic's strategy of offering below-market mortgages meant its assets lost massive value when rates rose. Wealthy clients had deposits far exceeding FDIC limits, so they quickly moved money to perceived safer institutions after SVB's failure.

faq.question: How did JPMorgan benefit from First Republic's failure?
faq.answer: JPMorgan acquired First Republic's assets at a significant discount with FDIC loss-sharing agreements. The deal added wealthy clients and a premium brand to JPMorgan's portfolio while the FDIC absorbed estimated losses of $13 billion.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-iceland.summary: Iceland's three largest banks collapsed simultaneously in 2008, owing $85 billion from a country with a GDP of just $14 billion. The crisis bankrupt the nation, destroyed its currency, and led to unprecedented citizen protests and government reform.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-iceland.whyItMatters: Iceland showed what happens when an entire country's banking system grows too large relative to its economy. The government could not bail out banks that owed six times the national GDP.
takeaways: Iceland's banking debts were six times the country's entire GDP
All three major banks failed within a single week in October 2008
Iceland was the only country to prosecute and jail bank executives after 2008

faq.question: How did Iceland's banks get so large compared to the economy?
faq.answer: After privatization in 2003, the banks aggressively expanded internationally, borrowing in foreign markets to fund rapid growth. By 2008, their combined assets were ten times Iceland's GDP, creating a national vulnerability that was impossible to backstop.

faq.question: How did Iceland recover from the banking collapse?
faq.answer: Iceland let the banks fail, imposed capital controls to prevent money from leaving, and prioritized protecting domestic depositors. The country jailed dozens of bankers, reformed its financial system, and experienced one of the fastest economic recoveries in Europe.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-japan-s.summary: Japan's banking crisis began when a massive asset bubble burst in 1990, leaving banks with trillions in bad loans they refused to write off. The resulting zombie banking system contributed to two decades of economic stagnation.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-japan-s.whyItMatters: Japan's lost decades demonstrate the catastrophic cost of allowing zombie banks to persist. Delaying write-offs and reforms turned what could have been a sharp recession into a generation of economic malaise.
takeaways: Japanese bank losses from the bubble exceeded $1 trillion
Banks kept lending to insolvent companies to avoid recognizing losses
Japan's GDP growth averaged under 1 percent for over two decades

faq.question: What are zombie banks and why are they dangerous?
faq.answer: Zombie banks are institutions kept alive with hidden losses on their books. They continue operating but cannot lend productively because their capital is consumed by bad loans they refuse to acknowledge. They crowd out healthy competitors.

faq.question: What lessons does Japan's crisis offer other countries?
faq.answer: The key lesson is to recognize losses quickly, recapitalize or close failed banks promptly, and avoid prolonging the pain through denial. The US applied these lessons in 2008 by stress testing banks and forcing rapid recapitalization.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-lehman-.summary: Lehman Brothers' bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 was the largest in US history at $639 billion, triggering a global financial panic that froze credit markets, crashed stock prices, and pushed the world economy into the Great Recession.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-lehman-.whyItMatters: Lehman's failure proved that letting a major interconnected bank collapse can cause a global catastrophe. The resulting crisis cost the global economy tens of trillions of dollars and affected billions of lives.
takeaways: Lehman's $639 billion bankruptcy was the largest in American history
The failure froze global credit markets within hours
The Dow Jones fell 504 points on the day of the bankruptcy filing

faq.question: Why did the government let Lehman Brothers fail?
faq.answer: Political backlash from the Bear Stearns rescue made another bailout politically toxic. Treasury Secretary Paulson and Fed Chair Bernanke have said they lacked legal authority for a rescue, though critics argue they chose not to find a way.

faq.question: What happened to the global economy after Lehman's collapse?
faq.answer: Credit markets froze worldwide, stock markets crashed, trade volumes collapsed, and millions lost jobs. Global GDP contracted for the first time since World War II. The resulting Great Recession lasted years and some economies took a decade to recover.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-long-te.summary: Long-Term Capital Management was a hedge fund run by Nobel laureates that used extreme leverage to make bets on bond markets. When Russia defaulted in 1998, LTCM's $4.6 billion in losses threatened to cascade through the entire financial system.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-long-te.whyItMatters: LTCM proved that genius does not eliminate risk. Its near-failure showed how a single leveraged fund could threaten systemic stability, foreshadowing the too-big-to-fail problems of 2008.
takeaways: LTCM leveraged $4 billion in capital into $125 billion in positions
Two Nobel Prize-winning economists designed its trading strategies
The Fed organized a $3.6 billion private-sector rescue to prevent contagion

faq.question: How did Nobel Prize winners lose so much money?
faq.answer: LTCM's models assumed historical patterns would continue and markets would remain liquid. Russia's unexpected default and subsequent global panic created conditions their models had said were virtually impossible, proving that tail risks can overwhelm any model.

faq.question: Why did the Fed intervene for a private hedge fund?
faq.answer: LTCM's positions were so large and so interconnected with major banks that its uncontrolled collapse would have forced fire sales across global markets. The Fed organized a private rescue rather than a taxpayer bailout to prevent systemic contagion.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-overend.summary: Overend, Gurney & Company was a Victorian-era London bank that collapsed in 1866 after reckless lending to risky ventures. Its failure triggered a financial panic that forced the Bank of England to establish itself as the lender of last resort.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-overend.whyItMatters: The Overend Gurney crisis defined the modern central banking concept of lender of last resort. The Bank of England's response created principles still used today when central banks intervene during financial panics.
takeaways: Overend Gurney's failure triggered Black Friday on May 11, 1866
The bank had shifted from safe discount activities to risky speculative lending
Walter Bagehot's response formulated the rules for central bank crisis lending

faq.question: What is Bagehot's dictum?
faq.answer: Walter Bagehot wrote that in a crisis, the central bank should lend freely at a penalty rate against good collateral. This principle, born from the Overend Gurney crisis, remains the foundation of how central banks respond to financial panics.

faq.question: How does a Victorian-era bank failure remain relevant today?
faq.answer: The Overend Gurney collapse established that financial systems need a lender of last resort. Every time the Fed or ECB makes emergency loans during a crisis, they are applying principles developed in response to this 1866 bank failure.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-penn-sq.summary: Penn Square Bank was a tiny Oklahoma shopping mall bank that triggered a chain reaction of major bank failures in 1982 by originating billions in risky oil loans and selling participations to Continental Illinois and other large institutions.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-penn-sq.whyItMatters: Penn Square proved that a small bank can cause systemic damage by selling its risks upstream to larger institutions. The failure demonstrated how interconnected banking creates hidden vulnerabilities across the system.
takeaways: Penn Square had just $525 million in assets but originated billions in loan participations
Its failure directly caused Continental Illinois to need a government rescue
Oil price declines turned the bank's speculative energy loans into massive losses

faq.question: How did a small bank cause such widespread damage?
faq.answer: Penn Square originated far more loans than it could hold, selling participations to major banks including Continental Illinois and Seattle-First. When the loans defaulted, the losses rippled through every bank that had purchased them.

faq.question: What lesson does Penn Square offer about banking risk?
faq.answer: Penn Square showed that risk in banking is about connections, not just size. A small institution can poison the system if larger banks blindly purchase its risks. Due diligence on loan quality must happen at every level of the chain.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-savings.summary: Over 1,000 savings and loan institutions failed in the 1980s and early 1990s after deregulation allowed them to make risky investments with government-insured deposits. The cleanup cost taxpayers $132 billion.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-savings.whyItMatters: The S&L crisis was the largest American financial disaster before 2008, proving that deregulation combined with government deposit insurance creates a moral hazard recipe for catastrophic losses.
takeaways: Over 1,000 S&L institutions failed between 1986 and 1995
Deregulation in 1982 allowed S&Ls to invest in risky commercial real estate
The Resolution Trust Corporation liquidated $394 billion in failed S&L assets

faq.question: What caused the savings and loan crisis?
faq.answer: S&Ls were deregulated to invest in commercial real estate and other high-risk assets while still backed by government deposit insurance. When real estate markets crashed, losses consumed the entire industry's capital and the insurance fund.

faq.question: How was the S&L crisis ultimately resolved?
faq.answer: Congress created the Resolution Trust Corporation to take over and sell failed S&L assets. The cleanup took years and cost taxpayers $132 billion. Stricter regulations prevented a repeat, though similar dynamics appeared in the 2008 crisis.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-signatu.summary: Signature Bank was closed by regulators in March 2023 after a rapid deposit outflow driven by its heavy exposure to cryptocurrency clients. Its failure, alongside Silicon Valley Bank, raised questions about the banking system's resilience to digital panics.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-signatu.whyItMatters: Signature Bank's failure demonstrated that concentration in a single volatile industry can be fatal. Its crypto-heavy deposit base proved to be a liability when the crypto market collapsed.
takeaways: Signature Bank had roughly 20 percent of deposits from crypto firms
The bank was seized two days after Silicon Valley Bank's collapse
Signature was the third-largest bank failure in US history at $110 billion

faq.question: Was Signature Bank's failure caused by cryptocurrency?
faq.answer: Crypto exposure contributed but was not the sole cause. The crypto winter reduced deposits, and SVB's collapse triggered a broader panic among uninsured depositors. Signature's concentrated client base made it especially vulnerable to contagion fear.

faq.question: What happened to Signature Bank's depositors?
faq.answer: Regulators guaranteed all deposits, including those above the $250,000 FDIC limit, to prevent further contagion. Flagstar Bank acquired most of Signature's deposits and certain loan portfolios in an FDIC-managed resolution.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-silicon.summary: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in just 48 hours in March 2023 after a failed stock offering triggered a social media-driven bank run. Depositors withdrew $42 billion in a single day, making it the fastest bank failure in modern history.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-silicon.whyItMatters: SVB proved that digital bank runs can destroy an institution at speeds that regulators cannot match. The failure exposed how rising interest rates create hidden losses in bank bond portfolios.
takeaways: SVB lost $42 billion in deposits in a single day
Its bond portfolio had $17 billion in unrealized losses from rising rates
93 percent of deposits exceeded the $250,000 FDIC insurance limit

faq.question: Why did Silicon Valley Bank fail so quickly?
faq.answer: SVB had invested heavily in long-term bonds that lost value as rates rose. When it tried to raise capital by selling bonds at a loss, social media-driven panic caused $42 billion in withdrawals in one day, far exceeding the bank's available cash.

faq.question: Were SVB depositors above the FDIC limit protected?
faq.answer: Yes. The FDIC, Treasury, and Fed jointly invoked a systemic risk exception to guarantee all deposits, including those above $250,000. This prevented potential contagion to other banks with similarly concentrated, largely uninsured deposit bases.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-193.summary: Between 1930 and 1933, over 9,000 US banks failed as depositor panics cascaded across the country. The crisis destroyed a third of the American banking system and deepened the Great Depression into the worst economic catastrophe in modern history.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-193.whyItMatters: The 1930s bank panics led directly to the creation of deposit insurance and modern banking regulation. Understanding this era explains why governments will go to extraordinary lengths to prevent bank panics today.
takeaways: Over 9,000 banks failed between 1930 and 1933
Depositors lost $1.3 billion, equivalent to over $25 billion today
The crisis led to the creation of the FDIC in 1933

faq.question: How did bank failures worsen the Great Depression?
faq.answer: When banks failed, depositors lost their savings and businesses lost their credit. Surviving banks hoarded cash instead of lending, freezing economic activity. The money supply contracted by a third, turning a recession into a catastrophic depression.

faq.question: How did the government finally stop the bank panics?
faq.answer: Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday in March 1933, closing all banks for inspection. Only verified solvent banks were allowed to reopen. Congress then created the FDIC to insure deposits, eliminating the incentive for panic withdrawals.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-asi.summary: The 1997 Asian financial crisis saw currencies and banking systems across Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea, and other nations collapse after massive capital outflows. The IMF bailouts totaled over $100 billion and caused severe economic contractions.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-asi.whyItMatters: The Asian crisis showed how interconnected global capital flows could devastate seemingly healthy economies overnight. It reshaped how emerging markets manage foreign borrowing and currency risk.
takeaways: The crisis began with the Thai baht devaluation in July 1997
Indonesia's GDP contracted 13 percent in a single year
IMF bailout conditions were criticized as worsening the crisis

faq.question: What triggered the Asian financial crisis?
faq.answer: Asian banks and corporations had borrowed heavily in US dollars while earning revenue in local currencies. When Thailand devalued the baht, foreign investors panicked and pulled capital from the entire region, causing currencies and banks to collapse simultaneously.

faq.question: Why was the IMF response controversial?
faq.answer: IMF bailouts required austerity measures including budget cuts, high interest rates, and banking closures during a severe recession. Critics argued these conditions worsened the downturn and imposed unnecessary suffering on populations that had not caused the crisis.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-ban.summary: The Bank of United States failed in December 1930, becoming the largest US bank failure up to that time. Its misleading name made many depositors believe it was a government institution, and its collapse accelerated the Great Depression's banking panic.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-ban.whyItMatters: Despite its name, the Bank of United States was a private bank serving mainly immigrant communities. Its failure disproportionately affected the poor and demonstrated how bank names can mislead depositors about safety.
takeaways: The Bank of United States had over 400,000 depositors when it failed
Its name confused depositors into believing it was government-backed
The failure triggered panic withdrawals at banks across New York

faq.question: Why was the Bank of United States not saved?
faq.answer: Other New York banks considered a rescue but ultimately refused, partly due to anti-immigrant prejudice since its depositors were mainly Jewish immigrants. The failure to save it was later seen as a critical mistake that deepened the Depression.

faq.question: How did the failure accelerate the Depression?
faq.answer: The bank's official-sounding name made its failure seem like a government default to many. Panic spread rapidly, triggering runs on other banks. The cascading failures contracted the money supply and credit, deepening the economic catastrophe.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-kea.summary: Five US senators intervened with regulators on behalf of savings and loan owner Charles Keating, who had donated $1.3 million to their campaigns. Keating's Lincoln Savings ultimately cost taxpayers $3.4 billion when it failed.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-kea.whyItMatters: The Keating Five scandal exposed how campaign donations could buy political protection for reckless banking. It demonstrated the dangerous intersection of money in politics and financial regulation.
takeaways: Five senators pressured regulators to delay enforcement against Lincoln Savings
Keating donated $1.3 million to their campaigns through various channels
Lincoln Savings' failure cost taxpayers $3.4 billion

faq.question: What did the Keating Five senators actually do?
faq.answer: The five senators attended meetings with bank regulators and pressured them to back off their investigation of Lincoln Savings. The regulatory delays allowed Keating to continue risky activities, ultimately increasing the cost of the failure significantly.

faq.question: Were the senators punished?
faq.answer: The Senate Ethics Committee reprimanded one senator, Alan Cranston, and found the others had shown poor judgment but committed no crime. John McCain, one of the five, became a prominent campaign finance reform advocate partly in response to the scandal.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-pan.summary: The Panic of 1907 was a severe financial crisis in the United States where a failed speculation attempt triggered cascading bank runs. J.P. Morgan personally organized a private rescue that stabilized the system and inspired the creation of the Federal Reserve.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-pan.whyItMatters: The Panic of 1907 demonstrated that a modern economy could not rely on one private individual to prevent financial collapse. The crisis directly led to the creation of the Federal Reserve System in 1913.
takeaways: A failed attempt to corner United Copper stock triggered the panic
J.P. Morgan locked bankers in his library until they agreed to a rescue
The crisis led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913

faq.question: How did J.P. Morgan stop the panic?
faq.answer: Morgan assessed which institutions were solvent and organized pools of money from banks and wealthy individuals to provide emergency loans. He famously locked bankers in his library and refused to let them leave until they agreed to participate.

faq.question: How did the panic lead to the Federal Reserve?
faq.answer: The reliance on one private citizen to save the financial system was clearly unsustainable. Congress concluded that the country needed a permanent central bank that could provide emergency liquidity and regulate the banking system systematically.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-sou.summary: The South Sea Bubble of 1720 was a British speculative mania where shares in the South Sea Company rose tenfold based on impossible promises of trading wealth. The bubble's collapse ruined thousands, including Isaac Newton.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-sou.whyItMatters: The South Sea Bubble is one of history's most important financial manias, demonstrating that speculative bubbles are as old as financial markets. Isaac Newton's famous loss shows that intelligence does not protect against market psychology.
takeaways: South Sea Company shares rose from £128 to over £1,000 in six months
Isaac Newton lost £20,000, equivalent to millions in modern currency
The collapse led to the Bubble Act restricting new company formations

faq.question: What was the South Sea Company actually worth?
faq.answer: Almost nothing in real business terms. The company had a monopoly on trade with South America but barely traded there. Its true business was a scheme to refinance government debt. Share prices were driven entirely by speculation and insider manipulation.

faq.question: What did Isaac Newton learn from the bubble?
faq.answer: Newton initially sold his shares for a £7,000 profit, then bought back in near the peak and lost £20,000. He reportedly said he could calculate the motions of heavenly bodies but not the madness of people, a lasting lesson about market psychology.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-spe.summary: Modern bank failures happen at digital speed, with billions in deposits moving in hours rather than days. Social media-driven panics and mobile banking combine to compress what once took weeks into a matter of hours.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-the-spe.whyItMatters: The speed of modern failures outpaces regulators' ability to respond. Traditional intervention tools designed for a world of physical bank lines may be too slow for an era of viral tweets and instant mobile transfers.
takeaways: SVB lost $42 billion in a single day compared to days or weeks for older bank runs
Social media amplifies fear faster than any communication medium in history
Regulatory response frameworks were designed for a slower, pre-digital world

faq.question: Why are modern bank failures so much faster?
faq.answer: Mobile banking allows instant transfers without visiting a branch, social media spreads fear in minutes, and group chats allow coordinated withdrawals. What once required standing in line now happens with a few taps on a phone.

faq.question: How can regulators adapt to faster bank runs?
faq.answer: Proposed solutions include real-time monitoring of deposit flows, faster emergency lending mechanisms, social media surveillance for emerging panics, and potentially the ability to temporarily pause digital withdrawals during acute crises.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-washing.summary: Washington Mutual was the largest bank failure in US history when the FDIC seized it in September 2008 with $307 billion in assets. JPMorgan bought its deposits and branches for $1.9 billion, wiping out shareholders and bondholders.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-washing.whyItMatters: WaMu's failure demonstrated that even the largest thrift institution in America could be destroyed by reckless mortgage lending. Its orderly resolution showed that the FDIC could manage even massive failures without direct taxpayer cost.
takeaways: WaMu had $307 billion in assets, making it the largest US bank failure
The bank lost $16.7 billion in deposits in the 10 days before seizure
JPMorgan acquired the banking operations for $1.9 billion

faq.question: What caused Washington Mutual to fail?
faq.answer: WaMu had aggressively expanded subprime mortgage lending and held billions in risky option ARM loans. When the housing market collapsed, loan losses consumed the bank's capital. A classic bank run in September 2008 sealed its fate.

faq.question: Why did WaMu's failure not cost taxpayers money?
faq.answer: The FDIC sold WaMu's banking operations to JPMorgan, which assumed the deposits and took on the assets. Shareholders and unsecured bondholders were wiped out, absorbing the losses instead of taxpayers. The FDIC fund was not depleted.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-who-pay.summary: Bank failures are paid for through a combination of shareholder wipeout, bondholder losses, deposit insurance fund assessments on surviving banks, and sometimes direct taxpayer bailouts when the failure is large enough to threaten the system.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-who-pay.whyItMatters: Understanding who ultimately pays for bank failures exposes the hidden subsidies in banking. When deposit insurance funds run low, surviving banks pay special assessments that are ultimately passed to customers through higher fees.
takeaways: Shareholders lose everything first in a bank failure
The FDIC fund is replenished by assessments on all surviving insured banks
Taxpayers become the ultimate backstop when failures exceed the insurance fund

faq.question: Does the FDIC fund have enough money to cover bank failures?
faq.answer: The fund held $128 billion in early 2023 against $18 trillion in insured deposits. It can handle individual failures but would be overwhelmed by multiple large bank failures simultaneously. In that scenario, the Treasury provides a backstop.

faq.question: Are bank customers indirectly paying for failures?
faq.answer: Yes. When the FDIC charges special assessments to replenish its fund, banks pass these costs to customers through higher fees and lower deposit rates. The 2023 bank failures resulted in a $16 billion special assessment on surviving banks.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-why-ban.summary: Banks keep failing because their fundamental business model of borrowing short and lending long creates an inherent fragility. Combined with leverage, confidence-dependent funding, and human tendency to underestimate risk, failures are inevitable.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-why-ban.whyItMatters: Understanding why bank failures are structurally inevitable rather than merely the result of bad actors helps set realistic expectations for regulation and prepares society for the next inevitable crisis.
takeaways: Maturity transformation, borrowing short to lend long, creates inherent fragility
Bank leverage amplifies small asset losses into existential capital shortfalls
Every generation believes it has finally solved the problem of bank failures

faq.question: Why is the bank business model inherently risky?
faq.answer: Banks fund long-term loans with short-term deposits that can be withdrawn at any time. This maturity mismatch means that even a perfectly managed bank can fail if enough depositors demand their money simultaneously.

faq.question: Can narrow banking prevent bank failures?
faq.answer: Narrow banking, where deposits are backed entirely by safe government securities, would eliminate the risk but also eliminate bank lending. It would be safer but would require a completely different system for channeling credit to businesses and consumers.

banking--famous-bank-failures--t-wirecar.summary: Wirecard fabricated $2.1 billion in cash that never existed, fooling auditor EY and Germany's financial regulator BaFin for years. The 2020 collapse was Europe's largest corporate fraud and a catastrophic failure of German financial oversight.
banking--famous-bank-failures--t-wirecar.whyItMatters: Wirecard exposed the weakness of trusting auditors and regulators to catch fraud. Germany's financial regulator actively protected the company from journalists and short sellers who correctly identified the fraud years earlier.
takeaways: Wirecard claimed $2.1 billion in cash held in Philippine bank accounts that did not exist
Auditor EY failed to directly verify bank balances for years
BaFin banned short selling of Wirecard shares and reported journalists to prosecutors

faq.question: How did Wirecard get away with fraud for so long?
faq.answer: Wirecard exploited Germany's national pride in having a tech champion. BaFin treated skeptics as market manipulators, EY trusted third-party confirmations instead of verifying directly, and investors ignored red flags raised by Financial Times journalists.

faq.question: What happened to Wirecard's former CEO?
faq.answer: CEO Markus Braun was arrested and charged with fraud. COO Jan Marsalek, believed to have masterminded the scheme, fled and is reportedly in Russia. The ongoing trial is one of the largest corporate fraud cases in European history.
